The messengers are a reality, and the best of them is the last of them, Muhammad ibn Abd Allah, may God bless him and grant him peace, whom God chose from among the Arabs, singled out above those before him with particular properties and distinctions, and whose religion He made the best of religions. For that reason a Muslim ought to acquaint himself with aspects of the life of this Prophet, his lineage, his distinguishing marks, and what relates to that.
That it is obligatory (wājib) upon all creation to follow Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace
In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.
Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds. I invoke blessings and peace upon him who was sent as a mercy to the worlds, and upon his family and his Companions, and upon whoever is guided by his guidance and follows his practice until the Day of Judgement.
To proceed: the Sheikh, may God preserve him, says: *And the messengers are a reality, and the Arab Prophet is the last of them, the highest of them in rank.*
To deny Muhammad is to deny all the messengers
Having mentioned the messengers, upon them be blessings and peace, and the obligation to believe in them in general terms, he goes on to the reliance placed upon the testimony that Muhammad is the Messenger of God, which is the second of the two testimonies; and these two are the two essential elements (arkān) of belief:
The first essential element is the testimony that there is no god but God, and every detail that has preceded falls within this testimony.
The second essential element is the testimony that Muhammad is the Messenger of God.
We only began, before speaking of this testimony, by speaking of the messengers because affirming the truthfulness of the messengers is included in affirming the truthfulness of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace. Whoever denies a single messenger has denied all the messengers, and whoever affirms the truthfulness of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, has affirmed the truthfulness of all the messengers, because he is the last of them and confirms what came before him, as God has described him.
It is for this reason that God, glorified and exalted, whenever He mentions a people's denial of their own prophet, attributes to them the denial of all the messengers, as in His words: {The people of Noah denied the messengers} (Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:105); {The companions of the thicket denied the messengers} (Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:176); {The people of Lot denied the messengers} (Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:160) — and so on. Every time He mentions a prophet whose people denied him, He mentions that they denied all the messengers, and that is because the aim of the message is in origin one, as God, exalted, has said: {And they were commanded only to worship God, devoting religion sincerely to Him as people of pure faith, and to establish the prayer and to give the zakat; and that is the religion of uprightness} (Sūrat al-Bayyinah 98:5).
It is for this reason that the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: (We, the company of prophets, are brothers by one father and different mothers; our religion is one.) This is the interpretation of God's words, exalted: {He has laid down for you of religion that which He enjoined upon Noah, and which We have revealed to you, and which We enjoined upon Abraham and Moses and Jesus: that you should uphold the religion and not be divided over it} (Sūrat al-Shūrā 42:13).
The distinction of Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, over the other prophets
But the testimony that Muhammad is the Messenger of God requires that he be distinguished from the other messengers, and it is for that reason that he mentioned it here. Belief in him was made a binding condition upon those who came before him and upon those who came after him. As for those who came before him, the covenant was taken from them that they would believe in him, by reason of God's words, exalted: {And when God took the covenant of the prophets: "Whatever I have given you of scripture and wisdom, and then a messenger comes to you confirming what you have, you shall surely believe in him and you shall surely support him." He said: "Do you affirm this, and do you take up My burden on these terms?" They said: "We affirm it." He said: "Then bear witness, and I am with you among the witnesses. * And whoever turns away after that — those are the transgressors."} (Sūrat Āl ʿImrān 3:81-82).
So then: the covenant was taken from all who came before that they would believe in him, may God bless him and grant him peace, and support him when he was sent. It is for this reason that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said when he saw a page of the Torah in the hand of Umar: (Gently, O son of al-Khattab! Were Moses son of Imran alive, nothing would be open to him but to follow me.) And in another report, which Ahmad brought out in the Musnad, the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: (Had Moses and Jesus witnessed my sending, nothing would have been open to them but to follow me.) For that reason Jesus, peace be upon him, when he descends as a just ruler at the end of time, will be among the followers of Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, and among those who act by his religion and his sacred law.
The establishing of the proof (qiyām al-ḥujjah) against one who has heard of Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace
Further, faith is definitely not accepted from anyone who came after him, even if he believes in all the messengers, so long as he does not believe in Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace. It is for that reason that it is soundly established from him, may God bless him and grant him peace: (By Him in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, no one of this community — Jew or Christian — hears of me and then does not believe in me, but God casts him on his face into the Fire.) There is disagreement over the meaning of his words, may God bless him and grant him peace: (hears of me). Many of those who hear this report among those concerned with the intellectual field say: the proof is established by the mere fact that a person hears the name of Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, and of his message and of the religion he brought — even if he heard of it in distorted form, as is the case with most present-day People of the Book and unbelievers, who have only heard of him in the way they have heard of the Buddha, for instance. Others held that what is meant by hearing is undistorted hearing, and that this is what establishes the proof; its meaning being that they come to know that he is a messenger, and that he is the messenger of the end of time whose religion abrogates all that came before. This is derived from the Prophet's description of himself, may God bless him and grant him peace: in the report of Jubayr ibn Mutim, with which Malik closed the Muwatta: (I have five names: I am Muhammad, I am Ahmad, I am al-Mahi — the effacer, by whom God effaces unbelief — I am al-Hashir — the gatherer, at whose feet people are gathered — and I am al-Aqib, the last to come.) This entails that whoever has not heard of him as he truly is, and to whom his call has not reached as it truly is, has not had the proof established against him by mere hearing. But this is a remote inference, set against the explicit mention of hearing in the preceding report.
In general, many subsidiary questions follow from this issue. Among them: the cursing of those unbelievers who died without the call having reached them as it truly is. And among them:
Whether their blood and their property are rendered lawful during their lifetimes if they have heard of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, but the call has not reached them as it truly is — as is the case with the unbelievers of this age of ours, many of whom the call has not reached as it truly is. Are their blood and their property rendered lawful by this mere conveyance and hearing that has taken place, or not?
As for declaring them unbelievers (takfīr), there is no doubt and no disagreement among people over it: they are definitely unbelievers, even if they heard of this sacred law in the distorted way we have described. Whoever is lax and does not so describe them, on the consideration that they stand in the position of one whom the call has not reached, has been excessively lax; because what they adduce and rely upon is certain implied meanings drawn from verses, all of them of the type of the argument from the converse of the text (mafhūm al-mukhālafah), such as God's words, exalted: {Indeed those who disbelieve among the People of the Book and the idolaters will be in the fire of Hell, abiding therein} (Sūrat al-Bayyinah 98:6). Some people claim that "among" (min) here is partitive, and that not all of the People of the Book and not all of the idolaters are unbelievers. But this construction is as far from correct as can be: min is explicative of "those who disbelieve", the explication being that they fall into two divisions: they are either People of the Book or they are idolaters.
The Arab descent of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace
And the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace — God sealed with him the messages of the messengers, and made him of this stock known as the Arabs, and for that reason described him as "the Arab".
The divisions of the Arabs
The Arabs fall into three divisions. First, the extinct Arabs — that is, those who came to an end and left no remnant; among them are Tasm, Jadis, Wabar and Jurhum. Jurhum are those among whom Ishmael, peace be upon him, became an Arabic speaker; but they perished and left no remnant when they acted unjustly within the sacred precinct and God destroyed them. It is of this that one of them, Amr ibn Mudad al-Jurhumi, says:
*It is as though between al-Hajun and al-Safa there had never been a friendly soul, and as though no night-companion had ever talked the night away at Mecca.*
*Yet we were its people, and the turns of the nights and stumbling fortunes destroyed us.*
Of the same kind are Tasm and Jadis, who fought one another until they wiped each other out; and likewise Wabar, which perished and left no remnant.
The second division: the true-born Arabs, who are the descendants of Qahtan. In the report which al-Tirmidhi brought out in the Sunan, the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, traced ten tribes to Saba ibn Yashjub ibn Yarub ibn Qahtan, namely: Himyar, al-Azd, Madhhij, Anmar, the Asharis and Kindah — these six being of the people of Yemen — and then the remaining four tribes, which are Lakhm, Judham, Amilah and Ghassan; these four went northward, that is, they went out to the north of the Arabian peninsula. These ten tribes are definitely of the descendants of Qahtan. As for Qahtan himself, there is disagreement as to whether he is Hud, peace be upon him, or his son; the majority of the genealogists count him as the son of Hud, and it is for that reason that Abu al-Tayyib al-Mutanabbi said: *To the sweet fruit of which Tayyi are the branches, and of which Qahtan son of Hud is the root; to a lord such that, had God given a nation glad tidings of anyone other than a prophet, the messengers would have given us glad tidings of him.* On the preponderant view, all the tribes of Qudaah are also to be counted among the Qahtanis, even though they settled among the Adnanis and made their lands their home; and it is for that reason that the genealogists fabricated for them an Adnani descent that is not sound, namely that Qudaah is of the descendants of Maadd. But the preponderant view is that Qudaah is the son of Malik ibn Himyar, so that they are of Himyar, for all their great numbers. Among them are the Banu Kalb ibn Ghamrah, of whom were Zayd ibn Harithah and Dihyah al-Kalbi, and they are tribes of considerable number; among them are the Banu Udhrah, who were famed of old in the Jahiliyyah for passionate love, and likewise the Banu Tayyi.
As for the third division, it is the Arabised Arabs, who are of the descendants of Ishmael son of Abraham, peace be upon them both, and it is these from whom the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, comes. The meaning of their being "Arabised" is that they were not speakers of Arabic and then learned it by living among the Arabs.
God's choosing of Quraysh
The Arabs, then, are of the descendants of Abraham, peace be upon him. Abraham, peace be upon him, was sent at first in the land of the Phoenicians in Iraq, then he emigrated to Syria, and he did not speak Arabic. He brought his son Ishmael, by the command of God, glorified and exalted, to Mecca. The first to be his neighbours at Mecca were the Amalekites; then, when they behaved outrageously in the sacred precinct, Mudad al-Jurhumi expelled them from it. Ishmael lived alongside the Jurhumis and married among them, and they are the maternal ancestors of his children. Then God destroyed them, and after them the descendants of Ishmael through Maadd ibn Adnan prevailed over the sacred precinct. After them Khuzaah prevailed, until Qusayy ibn Kilab expelled them, and from that date Quraysh prevailed over Mecca. The reckoning of the lineage of all these goes back, on the preponderant view, to Maadd ibn Adnan. It is said that Maadd had a brother named Akk, who is the ancestor of tribes that trace themselves to Adnan, being of the descendants of Akk ibn Adnan and not of Maadd ibn Adnan. The most renowned of the sons of Maadd is Nizar ibn Maadd, who had four sons: Mudar, Rabiah, Iyad and Anmar; and from these the tribes of Adnan spread. Among these tribes are the tribes of Mudar, and among them is Quraysh, which is the greatest of the tribes of Mudar by divine choice; for it is soundly established from the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, that God chose Kinanah from the descendants of Abraham — and in another narration: (from the descendants of Ishmael, Kinanah; and He chose Quraysh from the descendants of Kinanah; and He chose the Banu Hashim from Quraysh; and He placed me of the Banu Hashim in the most exalted station. So I am the choicest of the choicest of the choicest, and I take no pride in it.) Several rulings follow upon this divine choice. Among them: that their captives were not to be enslaved, neither in the Jahiliyyah nor in Islam. Among them: that their prisoners were not to be put to death in captivity after the battle of Badr, because the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: (No Qurashi is to be put to death in captivity after this day.) And among them: that the supreme leadership of the community belongs to them exclusively — and that is not a consequence of the Arabs' tribal solidarity in their favour; rather the tribal solidarity of Persia and the tribal solidarity of Rome were greater than that of the Arabs, and to those the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, sent word that they should submit, for he is sent to all mankind. What counts, therefore, is the divine choice and election alone: He is not questioned about what He does, and they are questioned. That divine choice is the thing in which God honoured them with the leadership, and He honoured them with what is greater than it — namely that He raised up Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, from among them. It is for that reason that Ibn al-Rumi said:
*They said: Abu al-Saqr is of Shayban. I said to them: Not so, by my life — rather Shayban is of him.*
*Men are raised high by fathers; and at times men are raised high and adorned by sons.*
*And how many a father has risen by a son to the summits of honour, as Adnan rose by the Messenger of God.*
The Prophet's lineage, may God bless him and grant him peace, up to Adnan
The Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, traced his own lineage up to Adnan, and nothing is established from him beyond that. It is established from him that he said: (I am Muhammad son of Abd Allah son of Abd al-Muttalib son of Hashim son of Abd Manaf son of Qusayy son of Kilab son of Murrah son of Kab son of Luayy son of Ghalib son of Fihr son of Malik son of al-Nadr son of Kinanah son of Khuzaymah son of Mudrikah son of Ilyas son of Mudar son of Nizar son of Maadd son of Adnan.) The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, stopped at this limit in this sound report. Nevertheless there has come, in a number of other reports and a number of transmitted accounts soundly established from a number of the Companions such as Ibn Abbas and Hakim ibn Hizam and other Companions who were genealogists, that Adnan is son of Udd son of Udad son of al-Humaysa son of Qaydar son of Nabt — or Nabit — son of Haml son of Ishmael son of Abraham son of Azar son of Nahur son of Abir son of Falig son of Arfakhshad son of Matushalakh son of Sam son of Noah son of Lamak son of Mahlail son of al-Yarid son of Akhnukh son of Anush son of Qaynan son of Shith son of Adam.
The genealogists have differed over the exact form of some of these names, such as al-Yarid, of which the form Yarid alone has also come down; and likewise al-Humaysa and al-Humaysa; and likewise Qaynan and Qaynan; and likewise Lamak and Lamk. These are differences in fixing the forms of the names because they come from different languages, so that the speakers of each language pronounce them in accordance with their own pronunciation. This is the lineage of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, on his father's side.
As for his lineage among the Arabs: five hundred mothers are known for the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, most of them Arab; and there remained no tribe of the Arabs in which he did not have maternal kinship, apart from the Banu Taghlib alone.
His maternal kinship in the Ansar and in the Banu Sulaym is well known, because he stated it explicitly. In the Ansar there is Salma bint Amr, the mother of Abd al-Muttalib, the grandfather of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace; and likewise in Sulaym, for he is the son of the Awatik of Sulaym. His Awatik are: the mother of Hashim, the mother of Abd Manaf ibn Zuhrah, and the mother of Abd Manaf ibn Qusayy — three in number — and they are Atikah bint al-Awqas ibn Murrah ibn Hilal, Atikah bint Murrah ibn Hilal, and Atikah bint Hilal: the younger, her paternal aunt, and the paternal aunt of her paternal aunt, in that order. This is what al-Badawi, may God have mercy on him, spoke of in his work on genealogies:
*The Awatik of the Prophet are the mother of Wahb, and the mother of Hashim, and the mother of the noble one,*
*Abd Manaf; and this last is the paternal aunt of the paternal aunt of the first, the younger one;*
*And they are, in this order, O man of standing: [the daughters of] al-Awqas ibn Murrah ibn Hilal.*
It is soundly established in the Sahih of al-Bukhari that when the delegation of Kindah came to the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, they said: (O Messenger of God! You are the son of Akil al-Murar and we are his sons. He said: We are the sons of al-Nadr ibn Kinanah; we do not trace ourselves to anyone else.) Even though, from the side of maternal kinship, he did have maternal kinship in Kindah, he did not wish to vie with people in worldly genealogies; for the boasts of Kindah are only of kingship and wealth and the like, whereas God chose for the Messenger, may God bless him and grant him peace, what is better than that.
The wisdom in the Prophet's being an Arab, may God bless him and grant him peace
There is disagreement over the derivation of the word "Arab". It is said: from arraba al-kalam, meaning to make speech plain, on account of their eloquence. It is said: from taarraba, meaning to dwell in the desert, because they are the nation that had no settled civilisation in ancient times. And it is said: from araba al-shay, in the sense of making a thing beautiful, on account of the beauty of their forms and faces, for they are among the most beautifully formed of nations. God honoured them by relating the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, to them; but He did not send him to them in particular — rather He sent him to all people. Among the points of wisdom in its being chosen that the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, the seal of the messengers, should be from the Arabs, is that the language of the Arabs is among the most agreeable of languages and the most expressive and clear of them; and for that reason it was chosen to be the language of this message, which is intended to be universal and all-embracing. For if the Qur'an were in the English language, or in the French language, or in any language other than Arabic, developments in the language would overtake it. Thus if the poetry of the English poets of a hundred years ago were put before people today, they would find that most of the words in it are no longer in use, and that many of the words used in it have changed in their signification and have come to bear another meaning. Whereas if you took the poetry of Imru al-Qays, who lived a hundred years before the birth of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, and put it before Arab children, they would understand its vocabulary — as in his words:
*Halt, you two, and let us weep at the memory of a beloved and an abode.* This stability entails that the significations of the words continue, and remain clear, across time. There is no language among the languages of the world with stability like this, except the very backward languages such as the language of China, which has no case inflection and no syntactic structure; rather speech in it is all single words, all of their speech being single words only. For that reason its characters number more than three thousand, whereas the letters of Arabic are only twenty-nine.
Mention of the messengers sent to the Arabs before our master Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace
The Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, is not the only Arab messenger sent to the Arabs; rather there were other messengers among them. Among the messengers of the Arabs are Hud and Salih, who were both sent within the Arabian peninsula, one of them in its north and the other in its south: Hud was sent in the Empty Quarter, in the land of al-Ahqaf, and Salih was sent in its north, at al-Hijr. Likewise there were other prophets among the Arabs, on the preponderant view. Among those named is Hanzalah, who is said to be the messenger sent to the companions of al-Rass. People claim that he was buried in a well in Sanaa, and that it is by the Great Mosque of Sanaa. This mosque was built only by the command of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, and its site was not known in ancient times until the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, sent word to Fayruz ibn Badhan that he should build a mosque for the people of Sanaa, and should make its prayer-direction between Nuqum and Ayban, and should place it between the rock and the garden of Badhan. Fayruz did that and built the mosque, and placed in it the two well-known columns, one of them called al-Masmurah and the other called al-Manqurah. The Companions of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, prayed in it, such as Ali ibn Abi Talib, Abu Musa al-Ashari, Muadh ibn Jabal and others of the great Companions; and it underwent enlargements afterwards, such as the enlargements of Ubayd Allah ibn al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib when Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, appointed him over Yemen. People claim that this Hanzalah was buried at a known spot in this mosque; but the burial place of none of the prophets is established, apart from that of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace.
Likewise among them is Khalid ibn Sinan al-Absi, for it has come in a report (that his daughter came to the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, and he asked her about her father, and she mentioned some of his wise sayings, whereupon he said: That was a prophet whose people let him go to waste.)
The final Messenger, and what God honoured and distinguished him with over those before him
The sealing of the message with Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace
But when "the Arab Prophet" is used without qualification, it refers specifically to the Arab Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, on account of his station and the majesty of his rank. He said: (and the Arab Prophet is the last of them), that is, the seal of the messengers, for God sealed them with him. The wisdom in the sealing of the messengers is that God, glorified and exalted, chose for humanity one single religion, which is the religion of Islam; but He knew that this humanity would pass through many stages in the phases of its life, as in the call of Noah: {And He has created you in stages} (Sūrat Nūḥ 71:14). So humanity passes through many phases: {You shall surely mount stage upon stage} (Sūrat al-Inshiqāq 84:19).
Hence, if the religion had been sent down to it and it had been commanded to follow it in the earliest phases and stages of its life on earth, there would have been a great deal of hardship in it. For if this sacred law that we have today had been imposed upon the children of Adam, much hardship would have arisen — such as the prohibition of marrying sisters, while mankind at that time was a single family, namely the offspring of Adam alone — and so on. So of the sacred laws there was sent down in each age what was suited to that age.
Yet in God's knowledge it was not suited to continuous application, until, when humanity had completed the phases of its life and reached its maturity, God, glorified and exalted, sent to it His Messenger, may God bless him and grant him peace, with this religion for which all religions had been a preparation, as He said, exalted: {Indeed the religion with God is Islam} (Sūrat Āl ʿImrān 3:19). So He sealed the religions with this religion, and completed it and was well pleased with it for all mankind; and it is for that reason that He addressed mankind with His words: {Today I have perfected your religion for you, and completed My favour upon you, and am well pleased with Islam as a religion for you} (Sūrat al-Māʾidah 5:3). Even so, God, glorified and exalted, took account in the legislation of whatever circumstances may arise; and it is for that reason that He said, after the sealing of the religion: {Today I have perfected your religion for you, and completed My favour upon you, and am well pleased with Islam as a religion for you. But whoever is compelled by severe hunger, with no inclination to sin — then God is Forgiving, Merciful} (Sūrat al-Māʾidah 5:3). He set out the lawful and the forbidden, yet even so, after His perfecting of the religion, He said: {But whoever is compelled by severe hunger}, that is, by hunger and the like, of what entails straitened circumstances; {with no inclination to sin}, not violating it; {then God is Forgiving, Merciful}. Of the same kind are His words: {And He has detailed to you what He has forbidden you, except that to which you are compelled} (Sūrat al-Anʿām 6:119). Hence He made the general rules and the established foundations sufficient for continuous development, so that the legislation can neither petrify nor come to a halt at a fixed limit; rather it will keep pace with the whole march of humanity, because of the generality and comprehensiveness of these rules — and God, exalted, has a wisdom in every particular of them. The sealing of the message with Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, is among the things necessarily known to be of the religion; so everyone who claims prophethood after him falls into unbelief by that, and is called upon to repent: if he repents, well and good; otherwise his neck is struck. God, glorified and exalted, says: {and the seal of the prophets} (Sūrat al-Aḥzāb 33:40); and in another reading: (and the sealer of the prophets); and the meaning of the two is one, because al-khatam and al-khatim both mean the one who brings to completion.
The loftiness of the Prophet's rank, may God bless him and grant him peace, above the messengers before him
He said: (and the Arab Prophet is the sealer of them, the highest of them in rank), that is, the highest of them in station with God, glorified and exalted; and that is because of his mastery over them all, for he said: (I am the master of the children of Adam, and I take no pride in it.) They all prayed behind him on the night of the Night Journey, and he is the intercessor for them all on the Day of Resurrection, so that the first and the last enter into his intercession. It is for that reason that, when Abd al-Muttalib named him Muhammad, it was said to him: Do you name your son with a name that is not customary among your forefathers nor in your tribe? He said: I hoped that the first and the last would praise him. And God realised his hope through the Greatest Intercession, in which the first and the last will praise him; for Adam and all below him enter into his intercession.
As for what has come from him, may God bless him and grant him peace, in his words: (Do not prefer me above Jonah son of Matta), and likewise what has come from him, may God bless him and grant him peace, when a man said to him: (O best of God's creation! — and he said: That is Abraham): the scholars have ways of construing that. They have construed his words (Do not prefer me above Jonah son of Matta) as meaning that a preference which entails disparagement is not fitting; rather all the messengers must be revered and respected, and none of them nor his station may be disparaged, for disparaging the station of any one of them is unbelief. For this reason it is not permitted that any one of them be described with a repugnant description, nor with what entails the lowering of his station or the diminishing of his degree. What is meant is not a prohibition of mentioning his own merit, may God bless him and grant him peace; but if the merit of the messengers is mentioned and then the merit of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, is mentioned, there is no prohibition in this.
Likewise his words to the man who said to him: (O best of God's creation! — and he said: That is Abraham): this was before God informed him of His choosing him for intimate friendship (khullah); for God had informed him that He had chosen Abraham as an intimate friend: {And God took Abraham as an intimate friend} (Sūrat al-Nisāʾ 4:125);
but his own knowledge of his being chosen for intimate friendship, may God bless him and grant him peace, came only after this. The proof of that is his informing us of it, for he informed us that God had made known to him that He had taken him as an intimate friend, and he said: (Were I to take an intimate friend, I would have taken Abu Bakr as an intimate friend; but your companion is the intimate friend of God.)
Intimate friendship is the highest station among human beings, because it entails that there remain in a person's heart no room for any love but the love of God; a person does not become an intimate friend of God until there remains in his heart no room at all for the love of anything other than God. It is for that reason that God reserved it for Abraham and for Muhammad, may God bless them both and grant them peace.
It is for that reason that the Sheikh said here: (the highest of them in rank), and used comparative forms, which entail sharing; for comparative forms only compare between two parties sharing in the attribute. So all the messengers, upon them be blessings and peace, are of lofty rank; but the highest of them in rank is Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace. It is for this that God took the covenant of them all that they would believe in him.
The distinction of the Prophet's miracle, may God bless him and grant him peace, over the miracles of the prophets
Then he said: [And each of them was given, when he came with the glad tidings, that by the like of which men believed] — and he is here versifying the report which al-Bukhari brought out in the Sahih: (There is no prophet whom God sent before me but he was given that by the like of which men believed; but what I was given was a revelation that God revealed to me. So I hope to be the one of them with the most followers on the Day of Resurrection.)
He said: *And each of them was given, when he came with the glad tidings,*
*that by the like of which men believed. But what the oft-repentant one was given was a revelation which God revealed to him;*
*so he has the most followers of the company on the Day the Hour comes, as he hoped* — that is, as he hoped, may God bless him and grant him peace. All of this is a versification of this report. His words (And each of them was given, when he came with the glad tidings) mean: God gave every one of the messengers, when he came (with the glad tidings), that is, with tidings of good, by which is meant his call, which comprises both tidings of good and warnings; for every messenger is a bearer of good tidings and a warner. Al-bushur is the plural of bushra, and what is meant by it is their giving good tidings of the religion they brought from God. (that by the like of which men believed) means: he was given such miracles that, had men seen them, they would have believed in him; for their miracles were dazzling, and every miracle, had men been gathered to it and seen it, would have established the proof against them. The religion that each of those messengers brought was suited to the time he was in; and for this reason their miracles were physical, establishing the proof only against one age — namely the age in which they were seen or were mass-transmitted (mutawātir). Then, when the mass transmission is cut off, the miraculous character departs from them. Thus, for example, the she-camel of Salih: there is no doubt that the proof is established by it against whoever saw it, or to whom it was conveyed by mass transmission; but as for us today, had it not come in the Qur'an we would not have believed in it, because we did not see it and its reports were not conveyed to us by mass transmission.
Therefore physical miracles go only with time-bound messages. As for the miracle of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, then in view of the permanence of his message it was this Qur'an, the abiding and everlasting, by which the proof is established against all people. It is for this that he said: (but what I was given was a revelation that God revealed to me); so his miracle is this revelation — even though he had many miracles, those miracles do not establish the proof against all people, whereas that which establishes the proof against everyone whom it reaches is this Qur'an, and it is the greatest miracle of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace. His words (that by the like of which men believed) mean: that by the like of which the proof is established against all people; and (men) means this human kind. *But what the oft-repentant one was given was a revelation which God revealed to him.............................*
Its meaning is: his greatest miracle, which God gave him, was a revelation that God revealed to him, and it is this Qur'an. Al-awwah means: much given to repentance and turning back to God, glorified and exalted; and this is praise of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace. God praised Abraham, peace be upon him, with it: {Indeed Abraham was oft-repentant, forbearing, and turning back to God} (Sūrat al-Tawbah 9:114).
What is meant is: the revelation revealed; because the verbal noun is applied both to the act and to that to which the act attaches. The act is the phenomenon of revelation itself, that is, the descent of the revelation upon him; and the Qur'an is what is revealed. So the Qur'an is called "revelation" in the sense of "that which is revealed", because it was revealed to him. And his words: ...*so he has the most followers of the company on the Day the Hour comes* mean: because his miracle is this revelation, he has the most followers of the company of the messengers, upon them be blessings and peace, on the Day the Hour comes. His words (as he hoped): this is what he hoped for in his words (So I hope to be the one of them with the most followers on the Day of Resurrection). This is soundly established from him, may God bless him and grant him peace: (For when the nations were shown to him, he saw the prophet alone, and the prophet with one man, and the prophet with two men and with three, and the prophet with a small band, and the prophet with a tribe; then he saw a mass that had filled the horizon. He said: So I say: Is this my community? And it is said: This is Moses and his people; but look to the horizon. And he saw his community many times over that.) This increase is a loftiness of station, because his reward increases with the number of his followers; for every single individual who believed in him — every act of worship he performs and every remembrance he utters — the like of its reward is written for the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, in a succession that is not cut off until the Hour comes. It is for that reason that his community was the longest of the communities in duration.
The testimony of the community of Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, against the other communities
Among the points of wisdom in the sealing of the communities with this community is that this community is God's witnesses against the communities on the Day of Resurrection. Now knowledge is a condition of testimony, by reason of God's words, exalted: {And we testified only to what we knew, and we were not guardians of the unseen} (Sūrat Yūsuf 12:81), and His words: {except those who testify to the truth, and they know} (Sūrat al-Zukhruf 43:86);
and in the report of Ibn Abbas, which al-Bayhaqi brought out in the Sunan with a weak (ḍaʿīf) chain of transmission, the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: (Do you see the sun? He said: Yes. He said: Upon the like of it bear witness, or else leave it.) Accordingly a person testifies only to what he knows; and yet this community are God's witnesses against people. Now had this community come before its time, it would not have been permissible for it to testify against the communities that come after it, because what comes after it would be of unknown report; so the communities preceded it in order that it might testify against them. It is for this that God said, exalted: {And thus We have made you a middle community, that you may be witnesses against the people, and that the Messenger may be a witness against you} (Sūrat al-Baqarah 2:143). And there is no prophet but his people will dispute with him on the Day of Resurrection, saying: {No bearer of glad tidings and no warner came to us} (Sūrat al-Māʾidah 5:19);
and it is said: And who will testify for you? And he says: Muhammad and his community. So much so that Noah's people dispute with him and say: No bearer of glad tidings and no warner came to us; and it is said: And who will testify for you? And he says: Muhammad and his community. So the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, and his community are brought, and Noah calls them to testify, and they say: Yes indeed, you remained among them a thousand years less fifty. And so they testify for him. No weight attaches to the great numbers of those who affiliate themselves to the distorted religions; for the religion of Jesus, and the followers of Jesus — their following of Jesus came to an end with the sending of Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, because Jesus is quit of them after he took the covenant from them that, when the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, came, they would follow him. And likewise the followers of Moses: by the mere sending of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, his followers came to an end, because he took the covenant from them that they would follow Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace. So all the Jews and Christians who come after the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, are not among the followers of Jesus nor among the followers of Moses; rather they are among the followers of Satan, for they altered the covenant that was taken from them all. Hence do not be deceived by the great number of those who claim today that they are Christians, and who claim that the most widespread religion in the world is the Christian religion; for this is not the religion of Jesus which he brought. Rather the religion of Jesus which he brought required following Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, when he was sent, and abandoning entirely what they had.
The questions
That the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, was not chosen from the true-born Arabs
The question: Why was the Prophet from the Arabised Arabs and not from the true-born Arabs?
The answer: As for the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, being from the Arabised Arabs and not from the true-born Arabs, this entails an increase of honour; for the Arabised Arabs are nobler and more excellent in the sight of God, exalted, and in the sight of people, even before the sending of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace. There is no doubt that the tribes of Adnan held the greatest station in the Arabian peninsula, so that none of the true-born Arabs could boast over them; rather they used to vie with one another in drawing close to them.
The permitting of the slaughtered animals and the women of the People of the Book, although their religion is not accepted
The question: If the religion of the Jews and the Christians is void (bāṭil), why then were their women and their slaughtered animals permitted?
The answer: As for the permitting of the women of the People of the Book and their slaughtered animals, and their being called People of the Book while their religion is not accepted with God, exalted — this is not an honouring of them; rather it is an honouring of the community of Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace. It is of God's honouring of the Muslims that He permitted to them the slaughtered animals of the People of the Book and their women, and made things ample for them, and placed no constraint upon them in religion. The People of the Book used to claim that they had a superiority over the idolaters, until the Sūrat al-Bayyinah was sent down, and in it came the words of God, exalted: {Indeed those who disbelieve among the People of the Book and the idolaters will be in the fire of Hell, abiding therein; those are the worst of created beings} (Sūrat al-Bayyinah 98:6);
whereupon Abu Bakr said: Their shoulders have become level, by the Lord of the Kaaba! So they have no superiority whatever over the idolaters: they are all of them the worst of created beings in the sight of God, and they are all of them bound for the Fire.
Rather their slaughtered animals were permitted and their women made lawful as an honouring of the Muslims, not as an honouring of them. They have no merit at all in that, as against the honouring of the Muslims by the permitting of these. For at the least, certain moral standards are shared between them and the Muslims, and they have an authority to which they refer, namely the authority of religion; and it is for this that the Muslims were permitted to marry their women and to eat their slaughtered animals. As for the other idolaters, they have no authority to refer to; rather they change their religion whenever they wish, and even their women could not be trusted in anything, because nothing restrained them. It is for this that Aishah, may God be pleased with her, said: [The women of the Jahiliyyah were of two kinds: she who would not turn away the hand of one who touched her, and she who had a secret lover;]
and in the report of Ali ibn Abi Talib: that marriage in the Jahiliyyah was likewise of two kinds. All of this entails an absence of faithfulness and an absence of chastity and inviolability; whereas these values are found among the People of the Book, in view of the values remaining with them from their distorted religions. We do not deny certain distinctions particular to the People of the Book in the rulings, such as what we have mentioned, and such as God's making those of the People of the Book who believed in Jesus stronger than all the unbelievers; for this is a distinction God guaranteed to Jesus: {and making those who follow you above those who disbelieve until the Day of Resurrection} (Sūrat Āl ʿImrān 3:55) — so they will remain stronger than the Jews, more numerous than them, and greater than them in worldly power. Hence, regarding His words, exalted, {and making those who follow you above those who disbelieve until the Day of Resurrection} (Sūrat Āl ʿImrān 3:55), there is disagreement among the exegetes over the meaning of His words (who follow you). Some of them said: what is meant by that is the disciples and the followers of Jesus, peace be upon him, who kept to his religion before the distortion and alteration — those who came before Peter altered Christianity. It is for these that God guaranteed this standing; and (until the Day of Resurrection) is not a guarantee that they will remain until the Day of Resurrection, but rather that all endings are at the Day of Resurrection.
And some of them said: what is meant by that is everyone who affiliates himself to him, even if the following is a mere affiliation, what is meant not being that he follows his religion; and on this basis there enter into it the Christians of our own time and those who come after us who claim affiliation to Jesus, peace be upon him. And there are certain other distinctions particular to them in the rulings, such as what is particular to calling them to Islam; for calling them is not like calling the people of idolatry, but differs from it in certain fundamentals, as in God's words, exalted: {And do not dispute with the People of the Book except in the best way, save with those of them who do wrong; and say: We believe in what has been sent down to us and sent down to you, and our God and your God is one, and to Him we submit} (Sūrat al-ʿAnkabūt 29:46); and likewise the informing of them of our belief in their messengers, and the like of this. So our calling of the People of the Book is distinct from our calling of anyone else.
Among the things by which they were distinguished is that whoever of them believed in the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, in his time is given his reward twice over; for it is soundly established from the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace: (Three are given their reward twice over: the slave who renders the right of God and the right of his masters; a man who had a slave woman and taught her and disciplined her, and taught her well and disciplined her well, then freed her and married her; and a man of the People of the Book who believed in his prophet and then believed in me) — that is, he was upon his own religion before the sending of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, and then, when the call reached him, he believed in the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace; such a one is given his reward twice over. This is a distinction, but it is one that follows upon entering Islam. This same distinction is also the one mentioned in God's words, exalted: {You will surely find the most hostile of people to those who believe to be the Jews and those who associate partners with God; and you will surely find the nearest of them in affection to those who believe to be those who say, "We are Christians." That is because among them are priests and monks, and because they are not arrogant} (Sūrat al-Māʾidah 5:82). Those meant by this are the ones who believed from among the Christians, and what is meant is not the Christians in their unbelief; and it is for this that He said: {And when they hear what has been sent down to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflowing with tears at what they have recognised of the truth. They say: Our Lord, we believe, so write us down among the witnesses. * And why should we not believe in God and in what has come to us of the truth, while we long that our Lord should admit us along with the righteous people? * So God rewarded them for what they said with gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein} (Sūrat al-Māʾidah 5:83-85).
These, then, are the ones who believed in the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace. The Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, foretold that a great number of the Christians would enter the religion, and he stated that the Jews are a people given to false denial. It is for that reason that he said: (Had ten of the Jews believed in me — and in another narration: twenty — they would all have believed.) Not twenty persons of the Jews believed in him in his time, even though he lived alongside them and lived among them; rather the Companions who are of Jewish origin are very few, and they have a very great distinction and merit, and most of them are testified to as being of Paradise, such as Abd Allah ibn Salam and Mukhayriq — because the two of them came out from this bigoted people afflicted with envy of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace; so their affirming the Prophet's truthfulness, may God bless him and grant him peace, and their believing in him and following him was a very great distinction, by which the reward is multiplied for them.
As for the Christians, a great number of them accepted Islam and afterwards entered the religion of God when their lands were conquered. There is disagreement over the distinction of the Jews and Christians who are Arabs: whether they have a distinction over the Jews and Christians who are not Arabs. One group held that they do enter into the distinction, because God's electing of this kind of people entails a choosing of them; and upon this certain rulings follow. Among them: that Umar, may God be pleased with him, did not impose the poll tax (jizyah) upon them as he imposed it upon others; rather he settled with them that they should pay the zakat as the Muslims pay it, and that was a cause of many of them accepting Islam.
This distinction was not made by the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace; rather he imposed the poll tax upon the Christians of Najran, being four dirhams upon every adult and four thousand robes a year — but he did not lay it upon them as individuals; he laid it upon them collectively, so that the poll tax was in the nature of a peace settlement, since the poll tax falls due upon every adult male, whereas the Messenger, may God bless him and grant him peace, laid upon them four thousand robes and did not count their numbers. Likewise the Jews of Yemen; and likewise the Jews of Khaybar after the defeat, for he confirmed with them the arrangement that they should take half the fruits of Khaybar and render half of them back to them, on condition that the poll tax be taken from them; then Umar expelled them. As for those who are Arabs, Umar confirmed them and did not expel them from the Arabian peninsula: he confirmed the Christians of Najran, the Jews of Yemen and the Banu Taghlib, and did not expel them from the Arabian peninsula even though they were adherents of a religion, while he expelled the Jews and Christians who were not Arabs.
In general this question is a point of disagreement, and upon this disagreement there follow rulings concerning the taking of the poll tax from them and treating them with a particular treatment.
The designation "People of the Book"
The question: Is the designation "People of the Book" applied to other than the Jews and the Christians?
The answer: The designation "People of the Book" is applied only to the Jews and the Christians; and it was applied in Sūrat al-Māʾidah to a third group, namely the group of the Sabians. There is disagreement over the Sabians: some people held that they are the Sabians of the people of Iraq and the people of Harura, and that these are a sect of the Christians who distorted their religion, like the Samaritans among the Jews.
Another group said: rather they are the followers of John son of Zachariah, peace be upon them both. But the preponderant view is that John had no followers particular to himself; rather he was a renewer of the religions of the prophets before him, a contemporary of Jesus, peace be upon him, and one who affirmed his truthfulness, as God informed us of that in His promise to Zachariah, peace be upon him: {that God gives you glad tidings of John, confirming a word from God} (Sūrat Āl ʿImrān 3:39) — so he is one who affirms the truth of Jesus son of Mary. Others held that the Sabians are the followers of Abraham, peace be upon him; and God has established in His Book that Abraham was followed by his people, and it is for that reason that He said: {Indeed the people most worthy of Abraham are those who followed him, and this Prophet, and those who believe; and God is the protector of the believers} (Sūrat Āl ʿImrān 3:68). His words (those who followed him) entail a plurality, yet none of his people believed in him except Lot and Sarah, and for that reason He said: {So Lot believed in him} (Sūrat al-ʿAnkabūt 29:26). On this basis his people did follow him, though we do not know where they settled. But the most preponderant of the positions in the interpretation of the Sabians is that those upon whom this name is conferred in the Qur'an are of the followers of the religion of Abraham; and some of his religion remained among his descendants, just as there remained among the descendants of Ishmael, from his religion, the hajj, the contracting of marriage, the full ritual washing (ghusl) from major ritual impurity, hospitality, and the qualities of natural disposition (fiṭrah).
In general, as for the Sabians existing today in Iraq, the preponderant view concerning them is that they are not People of the Book at all, even if they call themselves Sabians; and for that reason their religion, or the rites they follow, resembles to a great extent the religion of the Buddhists. Some people claim that it was one of the philosophers of the Muslims who named them Sabians, as will come.
The position of the majority is that the poll tax is taken only from the Jews and the Christians, by reason of God's words, exalted: {Fight those who do not believe in God nor in the Last Day, and do not hold forbidden what God and His Messenger have forbidden, and do not follow the religion of truth, from among those who were given the Book, until they pay the poll tax out of hand, in a state of submission} (Sūrat al-Tawbah 9:29).
Malik held it permissible to take it from all the unbelievers, and said: the basis for permitting the taking of the poll tax from an unbeliever is that he will be one of the subjects of the Islamic state, and that whole peoples, if they submit, cannot be put to the sword, so that there is no solution for them but the taking of the poll tax. It is for that reason that he held that if peoples are called and do not respond to Islam, but accept entering under its rule, then the poll tax is taken from them regardless of their religion. This is the position of Malik.
But the position of the majority is that the poll tax pertains specifically to the People of the Book among the Jews and the Christians, and the Magians are attached to them, by reason of the report of Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf: (Follow with them the practice followed with the People of the Book, without eating their slaughtered animals or holding their women lawful) — and in another narration: (or marrying their women). And there remained of the practice followed with the People of the Book nothing but the taking of the poll tax from them.
It is said that al-Mamun wished to put these people, who were in Iraq, to the sword unless they accepted Islam, because they are not People of the Book and he did not wish to take their poll tax. So they complained to one of the philosophers of the Muslims, who said: Claim that you are the Sabians. So they claimed that; and when al-Mamun wished to bring them to judgement, this philosopher came and disputed on their behalf and said: the People of the Book are not confined to the Jews and the Christians only; rather the Sabians are so too, by the text of the Qur'an — and he recited to him the verses that have come on that — and these are the Sabians. So he let them be; and from that time they called themselves Sabians.
Upon the foregoing disagreement there follows another matter, which is the matter of holding the blood of unbelievers lawful without a prior call to Islam. The position of the majority is that it is not lawful to hold their blood and their property lawful except after calling them. Ahmad ibn Hanbal, may God have mercy on him, said: it is permissible for you to attack the unbeliever and kill him even if you have not warned him; and he argued for that by God's words, exalted: {Then, when the sacred months have passed, kill the idolaters wherever you find them, and seize them, and besiege them, and lie in wait for them at every place of ambush} (Sūrat al-Tawbah 9:5);
for he says: one who lies in a place of ambush will not call out to the one he is lying in wait for and say: So-and-so, accept Islam or I kill you — because he has concealed himself precisely wishing to kill him.
Perhaps the position of the majority in this is the better; because the occasion of revelation restricts it, and in particular the expiry of the four months which God, exalted, gave as a respite to the idolaters after barring them from entering the Sacred Mosque, in Sūrat Barāʾah, in the ninth year of the Hijrah.
In any case, one ought not to be hasty in judging in the matter of hearing and the establishing of the proof; for it is among the things over which there is no disagreement in the community that the reaching of the call is one of the conditions for the rulings becoming binding. And the reaching of the call comes about only by way of the Muslims; as for its reaching by way of distorting media, the reaching of the call may not be fully realised by it.

flags.arabic: أما بعد: فيقول الشيخ حفظه الله :والرسل حق والنبي العربي خاتمهم أعلاهم في الرتب
flags.context: the opening line of the transcript, immediately before the commentary begins
options: the Sheikh, may God preserve him, says: (quoting the Sheikh al-Dedew, whose lecture this is)
the Sheikh — i.e. the author of the versified creed being commented on — says:
the Sheikh (al-Dedew) says, quoting the base text:
flags.note: The referent of الشيخ is genuinely ambiguous and it matters for attribution. حفظه الله is used of the living, which points to al-Dedew, and the transcriber is introducing him. But what follows the colon is a line of the versified creed being expounded, not al-Dedew's own prose; and later in the same text ولذلك قال الشيخ هنا: (أعلاهم في الرتب) unmistakably means the AUTHOR OF THE POEM, since the words quoted are the poem's. Rendered literally and flagged rather than resolved: choosing wrongly would make al-Dedew the author of a creed he is commenting on, or vice versa. The Sheikh's office can settle it in one line by naming the matn.

options: the establishing of the proof (qiyām al-ḥujjah) / the reaching of the call (bulūgh al-daʿwah)
the proof becoming binding / the call having arrived
the case being made out against someone / receipt of the message

jizyah, the tax on non-Muslim subjects of an Islamic state

flags.arabic: عواتك النبي أم وهب وأم هاشم وأم الندب / عبد مناف وذه الأخيره عمة عمة الاولى الصغيره / وهن بالترتيب ذا لذي الرجال الأوقص بن مرة بن هلال
flags.context: three lines of verse by al-Badawi on the Prophet's maternal ancestors among Sulaym, quoted from memory
options: translated as prose, with the last hemistich read as naming the fathers of the three Atikahs
translated as prose, with وهن بالترتيب read as 'and they are, in the order just given'
left in Arabic in the bilingual pane with an English gloss only
flags.note: Two difficulties. (1) The verse and the prose immediately preceding it do not agree: the prose names أم هاشم، أم عبد مناف بن زهرة، أم عبد مناف بن قصي, whereas the verse opens with أم وهب. The discrepancy is IN THE SOURCE and has not been reconciled (style guide 11). (2) The third line is elliptical — ذا لذي الرجال and the bare name الأوقص بن مرة بن هلال — and the rendering offered is a reading, not a certainty. A genealogist should check both before display.

flags.arabic: ولا يوجد في لغة من لغات العالم مثل هذا الركود إلا اللغات المتخلفة جداً مثل لغة الصين
flags.context: in the section on the wisdom of the Prophet being an Arab, arguing that Arabic alone is stable enough to carry a final revelation
options: except the very backward languages such as the language of China
except the very undeveloped languages such as Chinese
except languages that have remained static, such as Chinese
flags.note: EDITORIAL. متخلفة جداً means 'very backward' and has been rendered as such: the guide forbids softening (section 6). Option 2 is a euphemism and option 3 silently removes the judgement altogether, so neither is offered as the recommendation. The claim about Chinese that follows (no inflection, no syntax, all speech consisting of single words, more than three thousand 'letters') is factually wrong as linguistics, and it is translated as given, not corrected. Publication in English carries clear reputational exposure; the decision belongs to Ummah Collective and the Sheikh's office.

flags.context: reporting the Prophet's words, in the answer about the People of the Book

he stated that the Jews are a people of slander (buht)
he stated that the Jews are a people who deny the truth brazenly
flags.note: EDITORIAL. بهت covers both brazen denial and calumny, and the choice changes the force of the sentence considerably in English. The Sheikh is reporting a prophetic report, not stating a ruling, and the English keeps it as reported speech; it has been neither softened nor sharpened. The rendering should be settled by the reviewing scholar, and the record carries editorial_review for this and the surrounding passage.

translator_notes: A written-up lecture, filed by the site under the mohadarrat (lectures) category; typed "transcript", following record 1143. The text is complete: it runs from the khuṭbat al-ḥājah through the commentary to a closing position, and then a question-and-answer section (الأسئلة) with three questions. It is NOT marked source_is_excerpt_only, and there is no .docx or .doc download link on this page.

Record 717 carries the same title and the same opening, but is excerpt-only (805 characters, full text behind /medias/doc/L-35.doc). Its body is an exact prefix of this one. See the last flag; 717 has not been touched.
body_ar and body_en are aligned line for line — 102 lines each, headings included — so the bilingual pane can display them side by side without further segmentation.

body_ar is stored in Unicode NFC. The CMS serves some combining marks in non-canonical order (shadda before the vowel mark) in the vocalised Qur'anic quotations; NFC reorders these. The stored text was verified against the source by hash: NFC(source) equals the stored text exactly, and the character histograms are identical, so nothing has been added, lost or altered — only canonically reordered.

category_ar and category_en are derived from the URL alias mohadarrat (محاضرات, lectures); the page prints no breadcrumb, so the Arabic category label has not been read directly from the source and should be confirmed. Same convention as record 1143.

date_is_cms_upload is true. The page prints الثلاثاء, 12 يناير 2016 13:53 while the URL alias encodes 2016-01-12-14-01-03 — eight minutes apart, which is a save-then-publish stamp, not a date of authorship. The lecture itself is undated in the text; 717 publishes the same lecture with a 2011 stamp, which is further evidence that neither stamp dates the lecture.

The kalām exemption (style guide 8) was checked explicitly and does NOT apply here: every occurrence of وجوب / واجب in this text attaches to an act (following the Prophet, believing in the messengers, revering them, the rulings becoming binding), not to a proposition about God. The five-rulings mapping has therefore been applied, with وجوب rendered 'obligatory (wājib)' on first occurrence. الرسل حق ('the messengers are a reality') is a creedal affirmation and has not been treated as a ruling term.

title_en follows the rendering already used in the corpus at record 717 for the identical title_ar, so that the two records are recognisably the same text. Inside the body, شهادة is rendered 'testimony', which is why the title and the body differ in wording; if the corpus standardises one of them, both records should move together.

صلى الله عليه وسلم is rendered in full as 'may God bless him and grant him peace' at every occurrence, following the dominant corpus usage, and عليه السلام as 'peace be upon him'. The honorifics are not abbreviated or dropped anywhere, which is why the English is longer than the Arabic.

Lines of verse (the Jurhumi elegy, al-Mutanabbi, Ibn al-Rumi, al-Badawi, Imru al-Qays, and the versified creed) are rendered as prose in italics, per style guide 4. No rhymed English has been attempted.

Positions attributed to others are kept visibly attributed throughout: Ahmad ibn Hanbal on attacking without prior warning, Malik on taking the poll tax from all unbelievers, the majority (الجمهور) against both, and the two readings of 'hearing of the Prophet'. The Sheikh's own position is given only where he gives it — ولعل مذهب الجمهور في هذا أولى ('perhaps the position of the majority in this is the better') and the closing paragraph — and has not been read back into the earlier reporting.
editorial_review_reasons: The lecture poses, and deliberately leaves hanging for most of its length, the question whether the blood and property of unbelievers who have heard of the Prophet only in distorted form are lawful (استباحة دمائهم وأموالهم). The Sheikh answers it only at the very end, adopting the majority position that nothing is lawful without a prior call, and closing with a warning against haste in this very matter. Any partial display, excerpt, search snippet or social card drawn from the middle of this record will reverse its meaning. The record must be displayed whole or not at all.

It reports Ahmad ibn Hanbal as permitting an attack on an unbeliever without prior warning, with his scriptural argument, before rejecting it in favour of the majority. Rendered faithfully and kept attributed; quoted alone in English it reads as advocacy of unprovoked killing.

It states that anyone who claims prophethood after Muhammad falls into unbelief and is called upon to repent, and that otherwise 'his neck is struck'. Translated as given, neither softened nor glossed.

It contains sustained statements about Jews and Christians that carry clear legal and reputational exposure in Western jurisdictions: that Jews and Christians after the Prophet's mission are 'among the followers of Satan'; that the People of the Book and the idolaters are alike 'the worst of created beings' and 'all bound for the Fire'; that the Jews are 'a people given to false denial' and 'this bigoted people afflicted with envy'. All are translated faithfully and none is softened; several are the Sheikh's quotation or paraphrase of scripture and hadith rather than free-standing assertions, and the distinction is visible in the English but would be lost in any excerpt.
It disparages the Chinese language as being among 'the very backward languages', with supporting claims about Chinese that are simply incorrect. Translated as given; see the corresponding flag.

It carries material on the poll tax (jizyah) and on the treatment and expulsion of non-Muslim communities from the Arabian peninsula as historical-legal reporting; and, in the hadith of the threefold reward, a passage presupposing slavery and the marriage of a freed slave woman, together with Aishah's report on the women of the Jahiliyyah. All are faithful to the source and all are liable to be quoted out of context.
